mechanism: At T 1.0 the cued base loses problems it can solve by abandoning a line of attack that was working: after a first attempt it writes a thought-switch phrase ('Alternatively', 'Another approach', 'Let me try a different') and ends on the later, wrong line. RL-Zero-Math gives switch tokens much less probability inside a running attempt, so more of its answers finish on the first line they took.
starts_from: result-afc423 (43 % of the gap is base 3/4 -> RL 4/4, and the base's wrong samples are mostly on problems it solves elsewhere), result-a6ab7a (RL's advantage is already in the text by the halfway point). Built to explain why a base that solves a problem in 3 of 4 samples misses it in the 4th without a loop or cap hit.
differs_from: Unlike r2-revise-2 (weak error detector, refuted) and r5-m05 (restating after 'Wait', refuted), it is about leaving a line of attack, not about checking one. Unlike r5-m02 and r4-m02 (length as a readout), it names the token class that causes the extra length. m11 is about wrong values shared within one prompt, not about switching. m03 and m04 are about single-token errors, not about choosing between lines.
holds_against: result-855858 (check markers do not separate right from wrong samples): those counts are wait/hmm/actually, which hold on to the current line; switch phrases replace it, and nobody has counted them. r5-m02 refutation (base wrong samples are longer than their right siblings, +0.19 log): this fits, because an abandoned first attempt plus a second one makes a wrong answer longer.
base_change: Sample the cued base at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 with a logit penalty of -3 on the first token of switch phrases ('Alternatively', ' Alternatively', 'Another approach', 'Let me try a different') during the 600 tokens after each new thought starts (Wang et al.'s TIP). This adds no tokens.
first_test: On T1.jsonl (cued base, MATH-500, T 1.0), take the finished rows and count the case-sensitive matches of (Alternatively|Another approach|Let me try a different|Let's try another|a different approach) per 1,000 characters. Group the rows by k4, the number of right Day-1 #3 samples in math500_base_cue-01/rows.jsonl (attempt 0). Within k4 in {1,2,3}, compute the length-matched ratio of mean switch density in wrong answers to that in right answers, and the same density for T2.jsonl (RL) on the same problems. The mechanism is refuted if the pooled wrong/right ratio is below 1.3, or if the RL density is not below the base's.

mechanism: Loops under cooled sampling need a long, self-similar history, so they start only late in an answer. The finished-answer accuracy that T 0.6 buys (94 % of finished answers right, against about 90 % at T 1.0) comes from the plan and misread decisions in the first 1,000 or so tokens. The cued base's T 1.0 deficit to RL is therefore partly early tail draws at plan steps, which a time schedule can remove without bringing loops back.
starts_from: knowledge-13cff3 (on problems that finish at T 0.6, T 1.0 gets only 361-364 of 378), result-afc423 (first wrong step at a median 0.20 of the answer), result-34897a (gates on entropy over the whole answer bring loops back). Built to explain why cooling helps finished answers but hurts overall.
differs_from: Unlike r2-external-2 and result-34897a's gates (temperature by position class over the whole answer), the temperature here depends on time in the answer. Unlike r3-revise-2 (impasses come early under T 0.6, no claims), this says loop onsets are late. Unlike r3-surprises-1 (any tail cut brings loops back, failed), it says an early-only cut does not. m03 cools by token type, not by time.
holds_against: result-34897a (cooling only confident positions or only forks scores -1.4): those gates ran for the whole answer, including the late stretch where loops form; an early window leaves that stretch at T 1.0. result-faf15a (the base's wrong step is not an unlikely sample): that concerns slips and misreads in finished answers, while the plan-step gain claimed here is about which line of attack is chosen at the first forks.
base_change: Sample the cued base at T 0.6 / top-p 1.0 for the first 1,024 generated tokens, then at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 to the cap. This uses the same token budget.
first_test: In r3/base-01/out/F_math500.jsonl (cued base, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95), run rule A (8,000-character window from a line start, zlib ratio below 0.10) on every cap-hit text and record the onset character of each loop. Statistic: the share of rule-A loops whose onset lies before character 4,000 (about 1,000 tokens). The mechanism is refuted if that share exceeds 0.15.

mechanism: Olmo-3's tokenizer writes every integer from 0 to 999 as one token. The cued base's arithmetic slips are therefore single draws of the result token right after '=' or an operator, from a distribution spread over neighbouring values. T 1.0 draws a wrong value a few per cent of the time, and RL has sharpened exactly these result positions.
starts_from: knowledge-b748bb (every '0'-'999' is one token), result-f39ba8 and fact r6-account slip share 0.26 of the null-T1 gap, result-faf15a (RL lowers slips: D -0.72; W4 refuted because the span as a whole is not unlikely). Built to explain why slips persist at T 1.0 when the averaged wrong span is not a tail sample.
differs_from: Unlike r3-surprises-1 (tail tokens at every position, failed), only the result tokens after '=' are mis-tempered. Cooling them does not touch the connector forks that feed loops. Unlike r6-m06 (head-token swaps, untested), the error is a draw from a spread head, not a swap between two head tokens. m02 cools by time and m01 penalises switches.
holds_against: result-faf15a (wrong span log-prob -0.53 per token, against -0.63 for control text): a 29-token span average is dominated by copied context, and the claim concerns the single result token. result-34897a (fork-only cooling -1.4, cap hits 33): that gate also cooled the 'Wait/So' forks that drive loops, while result tokens after '=' are a few per cent of positions and are never part of a repeat onset.
base_change: Sample the cued base at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, except T 0.5 on any position whose previous token is '=', or an operator followed by a digit context, when the top-1 candidate is a number token. This is class-specific temperature scaling, and the token count is unchanged.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/wrongstep/math500-01/items.json, take the items labelled slip and compute (lp_head - lp_head_control) under the base model for each. Also count the share whose quote starts within 3 characters after '=' or an arithmetic operator. The mechanism is refuted if the median of (lp_head - lp_head_control) over slip items is above -0.3 nats, or if fewer than half the slip quotes start at such a result position.

mechanism: The cued base misreads the problem because its retrieval of facts from the problem statement weakens as its own solution grows between them. RL-Zero-Math keeps reading the statement, so its edge on misread steps grows with their distance from the prompt. A second copy of the problem placed close to the step would restore the retrieval.
starts_from: result-faf15a (Math 3.1 lowers misreads most, D -1.52, against -0.72 for slips and +0.03 for wrong plans), result-afc423 (misread 23 % of base finished-wrong samples, 17 % for RL). Built to explain why RL's error reduction falls on misreadings rather than on plans.
differs_from: r6-m01 (the deliberative register is held by attention to the cue and decays with distance) was refuted by the textbook-block count (0.007). This is a different variable: retrieval of problem facts, read on misread steps, with no claim about register. It contradicts m05, which says the wrong step is equally likely without the problem; 'twice' scoring separates the two.
holds_against: r6-m01's refutation (no textbook blocks late in long answers): that test reads register, which this mechanism leaves unchanged; a misread uses a wrong fact in the same deliberative voice. result-a6ab7a (RL's edge is already in the first half): first wrong steps sit at a median 0.20 of the answer, which is still hundreds of tokens from the statement, so distance can grow inside the first half.
base_change: Prefill, after the cue, a verbatim restatement opening ('Let me restate the problem: <problem text>') at the same T 1.0 / top-p 1.0. This costs about 100 tokens per problem.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/wrongstep/rules-01/items.json, for each item take r = (lp_span - lp_control) under 'twice' minus the same under 'base'. The mechanism is refuted if the mean r over misread items is above -0.1 nats, if it is not below the mean over slip items, or if its Spearman correlation with position over misread items is above 0. The prediction is that later misreads gain more from the second copy.

mechanism: The cued base's misread and slip steps are the continuation its language prior gives for a generic problem of this kind, not for this problem: they are about as likely when the problem statement is removed from the context. They are model errors at the mode, not sampling accidents, and contrasting the base with itself without the problem pushes them down.
starts_from: result-faf15a: W4 refuted, the wrong step has higher log-prob under the base than control text (-0.53 against -0.63 per token), so truncation and cooling cannot remove it. This observation was left unexplained by every graveyard theory, since r3-surprises-1 assumed tail tokens.
differs_from: r5-m09 (the base boxes a number copied from the problem, refuted) is the opposite failure: copying the problem rather than ignoring it. Unlike r3-surprises-1 and m03, the error is at the mode. m04 makes the opposite prediction on problem-dependence; 'noprob' and 'twice' scoring separate them.
holds_against: r5-m09's refutation (base wrong finals match problem numbers less than RL's, -0.043): this fits a failure mode in which the problem's specifics are ignored. result-855858 (6 of 11 base slips are followed by a check that repeats the slip): this fits too, since the same prior that wrote the step writes it again when the step is redone.
base_change: Use context-aware contrastive decoding at T 1.0. The logits are (1+0.5)·logit(cued base | problem) - 0.5·logit(cued base | same prompt with the problem text deleted), using two forward passes and the same number of generated tokens.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/wrongstep/rules-01/items.json, compute for each misread or slip item g = (lp_span - lp_control)_noprob - (lp_span - lp_control)_base. Also compute the mean change under cad1 relative to base. The mechanism is refuted if the median g is below -0.5 nats (the problem text is what makes the step likely), or if cad1 lowers the wrong span by less than 0.2 nats on average.

mechanism: RL-Zero-Math's finished answers are more often right because it ends with a substitution check: it plugs the candidate answer back into the conditions stated in the problem, which catches misread and setup errors. The cued base checks by redoing the derivation, which repeats the same error.
starts_from: result-855858 (6 of 11 base slips are followed by a check that repeats the slip; check markers do not separate right from wrong samples), result-96e819 (a self-review pass fixes no math). Built to explain why RL's checks fix errors when the base's same-rate checks do not.
differs_from: r2-revise-2 (RL detects errors better, refuted), r4-m06 (constant hold-on bias, no gain) and r5-m05 (restate after the hold-on, refuted: revision rates are equal) are all about how often or how well the model checks. This is about the type of check: whether it is grounded in the problem's conditions. m05 says the errors ignore the problem, and this says only a check that goes back to the problem catches them.
holds_against: result-96e819 (an appended 'Wait, before I finalize' review fixed 1 math error): that review re-read the draft, which reproduces the error; substituting into the problem's conditions is not what it prompted. r5-m05's refutation (revision rate ratio 1.04): equal revision rates after 'Wait' are compatible with different check types, because revising a number is not the same as testing the answer against the conditions.
base_change: Add one sentence to the prompt, used for both models: 'Before the Answer: line, substitute your answer into the original conditions of the problem and confirm each one.' Keep the cue and T 1.0 / top-p 1.0. This costs about 100 to 300 tokens.
first_test: On the finished rows of T1.jsonl (cued base) and T2.jsonl (RL), compute the share of answers whose last 30 % of characters match (substitut|plug(ging)? (it |this |x = )?(back )?in|check(ing)?: |verify(ing)? (that|by)) followed within 200 characters by '='. Report RL minus base. The mechanism is refuted if the difference is below 0.10, or if, within T1 finished answers grouped by Day-1 #3 k4 in {1,2,3}, answers with such a check are not at least 0.05 more accurate than answers without one.

mechanism: The 3.0 RL-Zero releases were trained with a 12k completion length and 3.1 with 16k. The 3.0 policies therefore learned to wrap up early: on problems whose 3.1 solution is long, they finish under the cap with a shortened, unchecked answer instead of hitting the cap. The 3.1-over-3.0 lead sits in the longest problems for Math as it does for Code.
starts_from: result-07f566 and fact r5-m08 (0.795 of Code 3.1's lead over Code 3.0 lies in the longest quartile), with r5-m08's review showing that Code 3.0 has only 5 cap hits, so cap hits cannot be the cause. The observation left open: why Code 3.0 loses long problems without hitting the cap.
differs_from: r5-m08 (masked truncations caused a runaway long mode that hits the cap) was refuted by its own 5 cap hits. This says the opposite: answers that are too short, not too long. r3-external-1 (3.0 keeps the base's temperature sensitivity, failed) concerns loops. m08 concerns error positions, not length.
holds_against: r5-m08's refutation (5 cap hits in 500): premature wrap-up predicts few cap hits. Fact: Code 3.0 is right on only 0.72 of the long problems that the base solves 4/4: the failure follows length rather than difficulty, which is what a length prior predicts.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/axis/math500-01/vectors.json (with manifest.json), compare the Math 3.1 cue arm with the Math 3.0 cue arm (allenai/Olmo-3-7B-RL-Zero-Math, cue). Sort the problems by t2_generated_tokens from per_problem.json into quartiles. Statistic: (Math 3.1 minus Math 3.0 in Q4) / (Math 3.1 minus Math 3.0 over all quartiles). The mechanism is refuted if this is below 0.45 (the cued-base gap's own Q4 share is about 0.36), or if Math 3.0 trails Math 3.1 by more than 4 problems on the shorter half.

mechanism: The Code-RL 3.1 weight change raises math accuracy by vetoing: it lowers the probability of the base's own wrong steps, at the same error positions where Math-RL lowers them, without installing Math-RL's replacement tokens. Code 3.0 moved as many tokens, but not at those error positions.
starts_from: result-eb9211 (Code 3.1 keeps the base's top token 0.667 of the time against 0.270 for taking Math's, yet scores 450 with the cue; Code 3.0 agrees with Math as much and gains nothing), result-faf15a (Code 3.1 D -0.45, Code 3.0 -0.32). The observation left open: token agreement does not order the models by gain.
differs_from: r4-m09 (Code's gain is only an ending policy, refuted) and r3-across-1 or r3-surprises-2 (a shared domain-general part, failed) say Code adds finishing or mode. This says Code adds error suppression at the same positions as Math. r2-revise-1 (Code's sign pattern is at chance, so no math gain) is contradicted by Code 3.1's gain, and this explains the gain without sign agreement. m05 is about the base prior, not the deltas.
holds_against: result-eb9211 (Code 3.1 mostly keeps the base's top token): a veto lowers the wrong continuation's probability and leaves the head token in place when the head is right, so the two fit together. result-faf15a's Code 3.0 interval [-0.95, 0.27] overlaps Code 3.1's: the mechanism concerns which items move, not the mean, so equal means do not contradict it.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/wrongstep/math500-01/items.json, compute for each of the 51 items and each model m the value D_m = (lp_span - lp_control)_m - (lp_span - lp_control)_base. Statistic: Pearson r over items between D_code31 and D_math31, and between D_code30 and D_math31. The mechanism is refuted if r(code31, math31) is below 0.3, or if it does not exceed r(code30, math31) by at least 0.2.

mechanism: Think-SFT's extra errors on easy MATH-500 problems are grader misses, not reasoning failures. Its teacher-trace final format (answers with units or words, several boxes, a final statement in prose) is one that grader v3's last-marker rule rejects on specific answer types. So the misses repeat on the same problems with and without the cue, and they are finished answers of normal length.
starts_from: result-bf6124 (at Levels 1-2 Think-SFT has 10 wrong against 2.0 for RL and 8.5 for the base, z 3.7, unexplained), result-0018d3 (v3's known misses are format forms). The observation is the unexplained easy-side excess in Think-SFT's difficulty profile.
differs_from: r4-m12 (the cued base's equivalent non-canonical forms are rejected on hard328) was refuted by 0 recoveries. This concerns a different generator, an SFT model imitating other models' traces, on easy MATH-500. r5-m04 (Think-SFT fails by cap hits on long problems, refuted) covers the long side, and this covers the short side.
holds_against: r4-m12's refutation (0 of the base's v3-wrong answers recovered by numeric equivalence): rule verifiers lose recall mostly on strong long-CoT generators, and the base is not one. result-dba8ee and result-0018d3 (second reads found no wrong answer accepted): those checked v3's false positives on base and RL rows, not false negatives on Think-SFT rows.
first_test: In wsp1/full500/sft1_cue-01 and sft1_plain-01 per_problem.json, take the problems the cued base solves in 4 of 4 Day-1 #3 samples (math500_base_cue-01 rows, attempt 0). Among the sft1_cue wrong answers there, compute (a) the share that are cap hits and (b) the share that sft1_plain also gets wrong. The mechanism is refuted if (a) exceeds 0.4, or if (b) is below 0.4; independence at sft1_plain's error rate on these problems would give about 0.1.

mechanism: RL-Zero-Math lowered its success on a small, fixed set of problems that the base solves reliably, problems unlike its training mix. The problems the cued base wins at T 1.0 are therefore persistent RL losses, not resampling noise, and RL misses them in most of its own samples.
starts_from: result-5e17a6 (base only 12, RL only 65 on MATH-500 at T 1.0), result-9b6af3 (a fresh base sample loses 35 of the base's right answers, RL loses 12), result-5de032 (7 base-only problems on hard328). Built to explain whether the base-only cell is RL forgetting or a draw.
differs_from: r6-account and its rival treat the base-only problems as a resampling null on one difficulty axis. This says a few are systematic losses. r5-m06 (RL raised existing paths, refuted on the rate) is about RL-only problems, not base-only ones. Unlike m11, no claim is made about the wrong values.
holds_against: result-5da8a9 (one axis; cross-arm excess union at most 1 point): a dozen persistent losses fit inside that bound and are a property of the RL arm, not a second axis across arms. Fact: random cell loses 35 against RL's 12: RL loses fewer overall, but this predicts that those it does lose are lost in all its samples, where the random cell's losses are not.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json, take the problems with t1 right and t2 wrong (cap hits wrong). For each, count RL's right samples among the 4 attempt-0 samples in day1_3/math500_rl-01/rows.jsonl, and the base's in math500_base_cue-01/rows.jsonl. The mechanism is refuted if RL's mean right count on these problems is 2.0 or more of 4, or if fewer than half of them have a base count of at least 3 of 4.

mechanism: When the cued base is wrong on a problem, its samples tend to give the same wrong value, because the shared prompt and cue lead each sample into the same misreading. Under a different opening the wrong values are different. This correlation, tied to the prompt, is why the 4-sample vote recovers less than independent slips predict.
starts_from: result-e41d94 (8 more 0-of-4 problems than binomial, and a vote 10 problems below the independent-slip prediction), fact r4-m07 (only 0.27 of RL's wrong answers equal a base wrong answer). The observation is the vote's shortfall, which no graveyard theory explained.
differs_from: r4-m07 (wrong-answer attractors from shared pretraining, which both base and RL hit) was refuted by low base-RL overlap. This places the attractor in the prompt context, not in the pretrained model, so it predicts low cross-prompt overlap within the base too. r3-surprises-1 (ties at random) failed. m10 concerns which model loses a problem, not the wrong values.
holds_against: r4-m07's refutation (0.27 base-RL wrong overlap): different prompts and policies give different wrong values, which is the prediction here. result-cbe0bc (shortest finished sample breaks ties well): ties exist only when wrong values do not coincide, and this mechanism says they coincide more often than chance.
first_test: Use the problems with at least 2 finished wrong cued samples in day1_3/math500_base_cue-01/rows.jsonl (attempt 0) and a finished wrong plain answer in T3.jsonl (grader v3 regraded). Let A = the rate at which two cued wrong answers agree (rln4_lib.agree) over all pairs. Let B = the rate at which a cued wrong answer agrees with the T3 wrong answer. The mechanism is refuted if A/B is below 1.3.

mechanism: Three solved examples in context help the cued base only on test problems of the examples' subjects. The base borrows the example's subject-specific routine (setup and the check that ends it), so the gain of a draw depends on which subjects its three examples cover. RL-written draw 1 happened to cover the subjects where the base's fixable errors are concentrated.
starts_from: result-5227b9 (same writer, two draws: draw 1 minus draw 2 is +6.3 points [2.6, 9.9], left open), result-afc423 (Intermediate Algebra holds 30 % of the gap and 19 % of problems). The observation is why one set of 3 texts gave 28 more right answers than another set by the same writer.
differs_from: No graveyard theory addresses in-context examples. Unlike m06 (the type of check, applied everywhere), the effect here is confined by subject. Unlike m11, it concerns gains rather than correlated errors.
holds_against: result-5227b9 (draw 1 gives 0.0 on hard328): competition problems rarely share the procedures of MATH-500 problems 0-2, so subject-confined transfer predicts no gain there. result-6d422d (base-written examples of the same 3 problems give +1.4 only): the base already applies its own routine, so only a routine it lacks, the RL-written one, can transfer.
first_test: In studies/rlneurons/results/axis/math500-01/vectors.json (manifest.json), take the RL-written-examples arm (draw 1) and the matching no-examples cue arm. Per problem, gain = examples - none, joined to subject from rln4/t1_t2_items-01/per_problem.json, excluding problems 0-2. Statistic: mean gain on problems in the subjects of problems 0-2, minus mean gain on the other subjects. The mechanism is refuted if this is below 0.04, or if under 60 % of the net gain lies in the matched subjects.
